<Rep. John Garamendi>: Following the passage of this year's National Defense Authorization Act by the House Armed Services Committee, I write to share my additional views and concerns with the bill as marked up by the full committee. The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 authorizes significant investments in our service members, military families, readiness, military construction, shipbuilding, sustainment, and the defense industrial base. I appreciate the committee's bipartisan work to provide for the common defense and to ensure our servicemembers have the support necessary to carry out their missions.
However, I must register serious concern with the direction of this bill and the broader defense posture it reflects. The bill autho1izes a $1.15 trillion defense topline while Congress also plans to advance another $350 billion in defense spending through reconciliation, with far too little specificity, accountability, or meaningful oversight. At a time when taxpayers are being asked to support unprecedented levels of defense spending, it is irresponsible for Congress to provide the Department with hundreds of billions of additional dollars while failing to demand basic discipline over costly nuclear modernization programs, politicization of the Department of Defense, and the executive branch's use of military force without meaningful congressional authorization. I am also disappointed that the committee failed to adopt basic guardrails for commercial data centers on milita1y installations. These shortcomings should be corrected before this bill becomes law.
FISCAL RESPONSIBILITY AND TOPLINE ACCOUNTABILITY
``An object in motion remains in motion.'' The term is as true in government as it is in physics. Year after year, we continue to increase our defense spending, reaching ever-higher levels. Adjusted for inflation, we are spending an amount roughly equal to what we spend in 1943. Such high levels are wholly unjustified today, particularly since this administration continues to claim, however unbelievable it may be, that we are not at war even as it requests ever larger budgets.
I remain deeply concerned with the defense topline. As this administration defunds humanitarian assistance programs, dismantles our education system, undermines access to healthcare, and chips away at hard-earned public benefits in the name of cost savings, the boulder of defense spending continues to roll down the hill, picking up speed as it goes, regardless of the damage it may cause. It is time for Congress to act: to cut wasteful defense spending, impose meaningful oversight, and reassert its responsibility to ensure that our defense budget is reasonable, accountable, and aligned with the needs of the American people.
A larger defense budget, standing alone, is not a strategy. It can mask mismanagement, reward cost growth, and allow troubled programs to continue without the discipline that Congress should demand. At a time when families across the country are asked to make difficult choices, Congress should not authorize enormous defense increases without a clear showing that every dollar is necessary, executable, and tied to real national security outcomes.
However Sisyphean may seem, it's time for us to push the boulder back up the Hill and restore balance. It's time to restore true congressional oversight. We cannot keep funding ever larger defense budgets with less oversight and be surprised when the president takes advantage of it. The first step to restoring that balance is for Congress to reclaim its constitutional role: demanding transparency before authorizing new spending, requiring accountability before expanding failed programs, and insisting that no administration, regardless of party, may use the military or the public purse without meaningful congressional scrutiny.
OVERSIGHT AND ACCOUNTABILITY WINS
Although I remain concerned with the overall direction of this bill, I appreciate that several oversight and accountability provisions were accepted. These provisions do not cure the larger flaws in the bill, but they are meaningful steps toward better congressional oversight and a more responsible defense enterprise.
I am encouraged that the bill includes important reforms to strengthen cost-growth accountability, including improvements to Nunn-McCurdy oversight and additional reporting on NNSA cost-growth compliance. It also includes F-35 accountability provisions requiring greater scrutiny of multiyear procurement savings and a reset plan for the F-35 global sustainment spares backlog. I am also pleased that the committee accepted provisions related to V-22 Osprey safety oversight, domestic manufacturing requirements for shipbuilding programs, limits on Jones Act waivers involving foreign entities of concern, shipyard workforce concerns, and contractor progress payment protection. I am proud to have joined my colleagues in adding an amendment that would improve the Departments Right to Repair by taking meaningful steps toward improving sustainment oversight, technical-data access, and the Department's ability to repair and maintain the systems it buys. These wins should be built upon, not treated as a substitute for the broader accountability this bill still lacks.
I am proud of my amendment to ensure that the Department of Defense can hold defense contractors accountable for poor performance. However, I am concerned that a provision included in the original bill would have effectively given defense contractors a veto over their own punishment. Whether the issue is price-gouging, poor performance, or the misallocation of taxpayer funds, the Department needs more tools to hold contractors accountable, not fewer.
NUCLEAR MODERNIZATION
As I noted in my additional views last year, I continue to have grave concerns about the direction of the United States' nuclear enterprise. When Congress considers weapons of this destructive power, our decisions must be guided by strategic need, fiscal reality, risk reduction, and constitutional oversight. This bill again fails to demand sufficient scrutiny of nuclear modernization plans that are growing more expensive, more difficult to execute, and less clearly connected to today's security environment.
For another year, the committee declined to provide the Department of Defense with flexibility on the statutory requirement to maintain a fixed number of intercontinental ballistic missiles. A rigid requirement to keep 400 ICBMs deployed and available is not a substitute for analysis. It deprives the President and the Department of the flexibility needed to adapt nuclear posture to evolving threats, arms control opportunities, resource constraints, and the demonstrated survivability of the sea-based and bomber legs of the triad. Congress should ask what force is necessarily to deter adversaries, not preserve an arbitrary number because it has become politically difficult to revisit.
The Sentinel Intercontinental Ballistic Missile program and the plutonium modernization program remain clear examples of why this oversight is necessary. Sentinel has already experienced extraordinary cost growth and schedule pressure, yet Congress continues to act as though continuing the program unchanged is the only acceptable option. NNSA has also repeatedly acknowledged the difficulty of meeting statutory pit production requirements, and independent reviews have raised serious concerns about costs, schedules, and execution. Congress should require credible life-cycle cost estimates, integrated schedules, and a full comparison of alternatives, including reuse and refurbishment of existing pits where technically viable.
I am also concerned by continued support for the nuclear sea-launched cruise missile, tactical nuclear capabilities, low-yield nuclear options, potential nuclear-armed hypersonic systems, explosive nuclear testing, and expansive missile defense concepts that could increase strategic instability. Congress should focus on reducing nuclear risks, preserving channels for strategic stability, and avoiding costly programs that invite arms racing without making the American people safer. As I wrote in a journal article earlier this year, ``Congress may have enabled arms races in the past, but a reinvigorated Congress has the authority and responsibility to reduce the risk from nuclear weapons. It's time we started acting like it.''.
POLITICIZATION OF THE MILITARY AND DEPARTMENT OF WAR RENAMING
I strongly object to the committee's decision to adopt language deeming references to the Department of Defense and Secretary of Defense as references to the Department of War and Secretary of War. The name Department of Defense reflects the proper purpose of the institution: to defend the United States, uphold the Constitution, and protect the American people under civilian control. Changing that name does nothing to improve readiness, strengthen deterrence, support servicemembers, or repair the defense industrial base.
Instead, this proposal is a costly and disruptive act of political symbolism. It would create administrative confusion across law, regulation, maps, records, contracts, forms, publications, information systems, signage, and official communications. More importantly, it sends the wrong message about the role of the United States military. Our military exists to defend the nation, not to serve as a political instrument or a branding opportunity for any administration. Congress has a duty to guard against the politicization of the armed forces and to preserve the professional, nonpartisan character of military service.
MILITARY INSTALLATION NAMES
By contrast, I was pleased that the Committee adopted language requiring military installations to be renamed in a manner that better reflects American values and honors the right people. This is a modest but important victory. Congress should not allow any administration to rewrite military history at will, restore honors to Confederate generals who betrayed the United States, or disregard the process Congress established to ensure that our military installations reflect the best of our country.
Names such as Fort Liberty, Fort Moore, Fort Cavazos, Fort Gregg-Adams, Fort Johnson, Fort Novosel, Fort Barfoot, and Fort Walker honor service, sacrifice, and values worthy of emulation by the men and women who wear the uniform. The names of our military installations should inspire servicemembers, families, and communities.
DATA CENTERS ON DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE INSTALLATIONS
I am disappointed that the committee rejected an amendment to establish basic oversight for commercial data centers on Department of Defense installations. Data centers are becoming critical infrastructure, but they also require enormous amounts of power, water, land, security, and infrastructure support. When such facilities are placed on or near military installations, Congress has a responsibility to ensure they do not undermine readiness, training, installation resilience, or community quality of life.
The amendment would have required the Secretary of Defense to certify, before entering into an agreement for the construction or operation of a commercial data center, that the facility had a clear military purpose and posed no risk to national defense. It would have required the Department to assess costs, continuity of operations, energy supply, water consumption, sound and light pollution, encroachment on training and operations, physical security, supply chain risks, personnel security, and the ability of surrounding communities to raise concerns. These are not unreasonable requirements. No installation should be asked to trade readiness, energy resilience, water security, or future mission needs for opaque commercial arrangements.
CONGRESSIONAL WAR POWERS
